🔹 Find duplicate rows using Pandas groupby() and filter()
🔹 Difference between merge(), join(), and concat() — with real-world dataframes
🔹 Fetch the 𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐝-𝐡𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐚𝐫𝐲 — nlargest() vs rank()
🔹 Employees earning more than their managers — self-merge logic with Pandas
🔹 Difference between apply(), map(), lambda, np.where() — and when to use what
🔹 Detect anomalies or fraud patterns using groupby().filter() and conditional logic
🔹 Reshape and pivot data — pivot(), pivot_table(), melt(), and stack()/unstack()
🔹 Working with datetime — parsing, extracting components, and time-based filtering
🔹 Year-over-Year or Month-over-Month growth — using shift() and pct_change()
🔹 Optimize Pandas performance — avoid loops, use vectorization and numba if needed
🔹 Real-world use of itertools, collections.Counter, defaultdict in data handling
💡 𝐓𝐢𝐩: Don’t just memorize Pandas functions — learn how to think in terms of DataFrames. AmEx wants you to write clean, readable logic — not hacky code.

ai_analysis.summary: This promotional post describes an American Express Data Analyst role for candidates with 0–3 years of experience and lists claimed Python interview questions without providing answers or worked examples. The technical coverage includes Pandas DataFrame operations, duplicate and anomaly filtering, combining DataFrames, salary ranking, employee-manager self-merges, conditional operations, reshaping, datetime processing, growth calculations, performance optimization, and Python standard-library tools. The post advises candidates to write clean, readable, DataFrame-oriented logic rather than merely memorizing Pandas functions.
subtopics: Duplicate detection with groupby() and filter()
Combining DataFrames with merge(), join(), and concat()
Second-highest salary calculation with nlargest() and rank()
Employee-manager comparison with a Pandas self-merge
Conditional and functional operations with apply(), map(), lambda, and np.where()
Pivoting and reshaping with pivot(), pivot_table(), melt(), stack(), and unstack()
Datetime parsing, component extraction, and time-based filtering
Year-over-Year and Month-over-Month growth with shift() and pct_change()
Data handling with itertools, Counter, and defaultdict
